readings.title: A repair cafe with long waits
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A volunteer repair cafe attracted people with broken household items. Visitors sometimes waited an hour before learning an item could not be repaired there. The main obstacle was no early assessment of repair requests. The team had limited tools and could not handle certain electrical products safely. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a record of items and waiting times. Volunteers counted common requests and listed the skills and equipment available each week. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated early information could prevent wasted visits. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a pre-visit checklist and a short triage desk. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: repair services must state their limits clearly. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in a repair cafe with long waits, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records.

readings.title: Sorting donated winter coats
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A reuse centre received many winter coats. Some good items were hidden in crowded boxes and were not taken before the season ended. The main obstacle was donations stored without size or condition labels. Visitors opened several boxes to find a suitable coat while volunteers struggled to restock shelves. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used a sorting trial by size and condition. Staff recorded which coats were chosen and where people spent the most time searching. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated simple categories improved both access and flow. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced clearly marked racks and regular quality checks. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: reuse depends on finding the right item. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in sorting donated winter coats, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Explaining a shared tool library
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A neighbourhood group lent tools for small home tasks. Members often asked for equipment that was already reserved. The main obstacle was availability shown only on a paper board. The board at the centre did not help people planning a task from home. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used a review of reservations and repeated calls. Volunteers asked members which information they needed before travelling. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated current availability was the first question. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a simple updated booking list with telephone access. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: sharing works when access is predictable. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in explaining a shared tool library, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A school uniform exchange
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Parents organised an exchange of school uniforms. Many families wanted to participate but found that donated items lacked size labels. The main obstacle was clothes mixed without accurate sizes. Some labels had faded, and different makers used sizes that did not match. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used measurements and a trial exchange day. Volunteers grouped garments by actual measurements and noted which descriptions caused confusion. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated measured categories made choices easier. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced size guides and separate condition notes. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: reuse succeeds through clear practical information. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in a school uniform exchange, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
When a community changes the community repair and reuse programme, a short explanation can be as important as the change itself. People want to know what problem was noticed, how information was gathered and why one option was selected. For a project about reuse and repair in everyday life, staff observed actual use rather than relying only on a drawing or an early promise. The evidence revealed an obstacle that was not obvious at first. Organizers made a limited adjustment and told residents when it would be reviewed. They also described the limits of the trial, because a small number of visits cannot represent every future situation. An honest account made the decision easier to question and improve.

translation.referenceAnswer: 社区调整一项服务时，简短解释可能和改动本身同样重要。人们想知道发现了什么问题、如何收集信息，以及为何选择某个方案。在一个有关循环利用与物品维修的项目中，工作人员观察实际使用，而不只依靠图纸或最初的承诺。证据揭示了起初并不明显的障碍。组织者作出有限调整，并告知居民何时重新评估。他们也说明试行的局限，因为少量使用经历不能代表未来所有情况。诚实的说明让这项决定更容易被讨论和改进。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the community repair team suggesting a practical change to the community repair and reuse programme. Describe who should be consulted, how the change could be tried, and when it should be reviewed.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the community repair and reuse programme. People have noticed no early assessment of repair requests, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
